stories.title_en: Saving 100 terabytes of memory by optimizing 1.1.1.1's DNS cache

comments.author: lpapez
comments.text: This is the right way to deliver software. Produce working product first, validate the idea, stabilize the business, start generating profit, and then you can start optimizing your costs. In fact optimization is by far the easiest part of the process because there are many system programming experts on this HN thread who consider these optimizations to be trivial.

comments.author: BikiniPrince
comments.text: Funny thing about cloudflare. I have a dns warming script that uses their top 1k or 10k addresses. Then when my master starts up it warms the entire cache. Everything else uses memcache so the cluster is nice and toasty. As far as I can tell no one else releases domain statistics like them.

comments.author: strenholme
comments.text: With my own MaraDNS, I aggressively optimized the memory usage of blacklist entries by having a single really big malloc() to allocate the memory for the entries, then traversing that memory block for potentially blacklisted entries. When I was using one malloc() per entry, a large blacklist took up 237 megabytes of memory. The same blacklist, once optimized to be loaded with a single malloc() call, only took up 9.5 megabytes of memory. https://samboy.github.io/blog/entries/MaraDNS.html#BlogEntry...

comments.author: vinkelhake
comments.text: These seem like some fairly standard approaches for reducing memory usage. I can't help to think that the approach of joining several distinct list into a single one in some way undercuts Rust's safety guarantees. If you previous had three distinct Vec objects, then Rust would guarantee that you can't index out of bounds. If you now put all those objects into a single Vec and rely on offsets, then you now open the door to indexing out of range of these sub-slices without any panics. It's a minor point, and it doesn't really invalidate the optimization, but I'm surprised the article didn't mention it.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、製品をリリースして利益を上げた後にメモリ最適化を行うべきという考え方と、具体的な最適化手法（キャッシュエントリとレコードデータを連続配置、単一の大きなmallocで確保、複数のリストを1つのVecに統合）についての議論だった。  
賛否両論として、最適化自体は「 trivial 」と見なす声がある一方で、Rustではリストを結合すると境界チェックが失われ安全性が損なわれる可能性があると指摘する意見があり、C言語では単純だがRustでは注意が必要という点で意見が分かれた。  
注目コメントでは、MaraDNSの作者が単一mallocでブラックリストのメモリ使用量を237 MBから9.5 MBに削減した事例を紹介し、実際の効果を示したリンクが共有されたことが挙げられる。また、Cloudflareのドメイン統計公開やDNSウォーミングスクリプトの活用例も言及され、実際の運用における最適化の事例として関心を集めた。
stories.editor_note: Cloudflareの1.1.1.1がDNSキャッシュのアルゴリズムを見直し、メモリ使用量を100TB削減した件は、エッジコンピューティングにおけるリソース効率の重要性を再認識させ、日本の通信事業者も同様の最適化を検討すべきタイミングです。

comments.author: sandcat_
comments.text: To provide one additional anecdote: I came off escitalopram with no taper after taking it for about five years (10mg). I got brain zaps for a while, got very irritated at times, but largely was fine after a few weeks. Not downplaying the withdrawal effects for some people, but they’re not as catastrophic as this article suggests for many (perhaps most). And overall I’m very glad I took it! It got me through a rough patch, and seems (in combination with therapy, and some life changes) to have rewired me a little. Symptoms I had for a decade prior have not returned. And I’m not sure I could have made those life changes without it. Sadly my arachnophobia came back though. Oh well.

comments.author: D-Machine
comments.text: Best way to manage the withdrawal would be to dramatically reduce them being prescribed in the first place. The linked article says they have "small to moderate effectiveness", but this is being far too generous. The correct way to measure drug effectiveness is if the treatment meets the standard of a minimal important difference. I.e. you measure depression on various rating scales, like the 17-point HAM-D, and research suggests a minimal important difference (i.e. one patients and clinicians can actually notice) needs to be about 3-5 points. But the average effects of almost all antidepressants do not meet these thresholds, i.e. the effect actually appears practically invisible. [1] Then you'll get waffling like "oh, but it really has a big effect for some people", but, well, no, we've looked at that too, and the placebo groups get just as miraculous "big effects", i.e. evidence supporting the idea "they really help some people" is also largely lacking [2-3]. All the other attempted saves ("oh, but eventually you find one that works for you") are also not really well supported either [4]. Like, maybe they really help some people, but it is far, far less clear than most assume, and should be balanced with concerns like withdrawal and serious side effects like emotional blunting and sexual dysfunction. EDIT: And just to be clear to anyone doing a drive-by downvote thinking this is about recent asinine US politics, it emphatically isn't. There are serious methodological concerns here that desperately need to be communicated to the public. [1] https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593736/ [2] https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7451660/ [3] https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33175895/ [4] https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11844611/

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、抗うつ薬（特にSSRI）の中止時の離脱症状についての実体験と、その症状の重さに対する認識の違いである。コメント主はエスシタロプラム5年服用後に急に断薬し、脳内電撃様感覚やイライラはあったが数週間で回復し、総じて薬の効果に感謝しているとし、離脱が「 katastrofic 」ではないと主張する。一方で、S NRIも同様かそれ以上の離脱リスクがあることや、薬の処方を最初から減らすべきだという意見も示される。賛否両論として、離脱が軽微で薬が人生の転機を助けたという肯定的視点と、薬の実際の有効性が統計的に臨床的に意味のある改善（HAM-Dで3‑5点）を満たさず、プラセボと同等の効果しか示されず、副作用や離脱リスクと天秤にかけるべきだという批判的視点が対立している。注目コメントは、薬効の測定基準として最小重要差異を用い、ほとんどの抗うつ薬がこの基準に達しないことを論じ、さらにプラセボ群でも同様の「大きな効果」が見られることを挙げ、効果の証拠が乏しいことを指摘している点である。
stories.editor_note: 抗うつ薬離脱症状への対応が臨床現場でようやく体系化され始めたのは、長年の患者苦慮を解消するだけでなく、製薬会社と医療機関の連携モデルとして日本でも注目される転換点です。

comments.author: NitpickLawyer
comments.text: > But I also think the demand for "fast/cheap/good-enough" models is just about to take off. There's a sort of "revelation" I had in ~early '24 when I used a 7B local model with a library called Guidance (initially out of MS, then the team moved) to create a flow where the model would receive pseudocode for tests, first write the tests, and once I approved then started writing code until the tests passed. This was before "thinking" models, and yet using that library I was able to "guide" the model in the required "prompt / instruct" context such that it was working towards completion, and I saw the first things like we see now in the thinking traces "oh, test x doesn't pass because blah, I need to..." and so on. Anyway, the revelation was "even if the models never improve, I'll have years of fun finding out all the ways I can use these things". And, obviously, the models improved a lot since then. But I think that revelation can still be applied, as a sort of "truism". We have, right now, access to things that 10-20 years ago would be considered magic. We are still finding ways of cobbling together systems with glue, duct tape and prayers and find new things they can do. I think the "good-enough" stage has come not just for API models (cheap, fast, etc) but for local as well. Even if slower, even if clunkier, but they are good enough for a set of ever increasing tasks, and what's more it's incredibly fun to work with them.

comments.author: michael0church
comments.text: It makes sense that we’ll see “room at the bottom” strategies. Currently, large parameter counts seem to be slush funds of world knowledge, language skills (because language’s nuances and open vocabulary make it high-dimensional), and reasoning primitives, the general belief being that the latter takes up the least space in the model. There are many applications where world knowledge is unnecessary or even a negative, and in which only a small amount of language skill is necessary, and there we can expect small models more intelligently used to beat large ones naively used.

comments.author: Lucasoato
comments.text: I’ve tested at least 20 STT models in a benchmark I’ve set up with German, Italian and English voices from meetings in my company. The voices contained very industry specific words, the languages changed from one sentence to another, sometimes words in a language were mentioned while a discussion was in another. The only local model that satisfies me is Voxtral Mini 3b, the only paid API that is slightly better is eleven labs. Yes, Voxtral might not reach the best score in the benchmarks, but to me, it just solves a problem. It might not be the best in terms of speed... but that’s not a problem for me. Happy to test this new model from Google but I’m not sure I’d go with that instead of something that can run so easily in my machine.

comments.author: hadlock
comments.text: What is really interesting for me is that they're not using Nvidia's Issac, which is famously impossible to get up and running for a custom robot by individual contributors. I can't tell how good their system is, but the fact that I got it running on my laptop in under an hour, vs wasting over a week of my spare time on Issac (ref: countless reddit threads by hundreds of people also failing to train their robot on Issac) gives me confidence I can finally convert my terrible IK stuff on my robot, to use this other framework. This appears to be using mjlab, which is is MuJoCo Warp plus rsl_rl, which uses a completely different design/technology heritage from Issac, so that's worth a lot to me, since I've basically sworn off Issac for robot gait training.

主な議論点は、公開されたOpenTIEとOpenXWAというタイ・ファイターおよびX‑ウィング・アライアンスの現代版ポートについての期待と関心です。コメントでは、オリジナルのタイ・ファイターをX‑ウィング・アライアンスのエンジンに移植した総変換Mod（TFTC）や、GOGでまだ購入可能なオリジナル版への言及がなされ、エミュレーションや公式リリーストへのアクセス手段が話題に上がっています。さらに、二つのバージョンを統合できる機能が「キラー機能」として強調され、かつてのファンが現代のHOTAS（ハンド・オン・スロットル・アンド・スティック）環境を用意して没入プレイを楽しみたいという意見も見られました。

賛否両論については、具体的な批判や懸念はほとんど見られず、ほぼ全員が肯定的な反応を示しています。ただ、一部のコメントでは最新のHOTASデバイスを入手する必要がある点が実務的なハードルとして挙げられており、これが導入の障壁になる可能性が指摘されています。

注目コメントとして、「Being able to merge the two versions together is a killer feature.」という意見が際立ちます。これは、二つのゲームシステムを統合できる点が最も魅力的であり、ファンにとって新たなプレイ体験を提供する鍵になると強調しています。また、「May need to find a modern HOTAS setup and immerse myself in these.」という声は、過去の思い出を現代のデバイスで再現したいという熱意を示しており、コミュニティのノスタルジーと新技術への期待が共存していることを表しています。
stories.editor_note: OpenTIEとOpenXWAはクラシックな宇宙シューティングゲームを現代のプラットフォームに移植し、レトロゲーム愛好家だけでなく、日本のインディーデベロッパーにもオープンソース移植の手法を示す好例です。

Smart aspiring blackhats will be targeting tmux next, both with light llm jailbreaks, light supply chain attacks (web search results) and LPEs within certain environments which weren't particularly useful before but with agents running on auto mode for hours become a very valuable springboard. 主な議論点は、AIを使った振動コード（vibe‑coded）ファザーがFFmpegで見つけたゼロ除算バグが実際の脆弱性なのか、それとも特殊なAVIOモジュールを制御した場合のみクラッシュさせられるデモンストレーションに過ぎないかという点だった。  

賛否両論として、AIエージェントは疲れ知らずで広範な知識を持ち、人間開発者のコストをかけずにバグ hunt を自動化できるため、品質向上に寄与すると評価する声があった。一方で、見つかった問題が実際の攻撃ベクトルではないと指摘され、AIが生成したハーネスはインターンレベルの作業であり、誤検出や悪用のリスク（例：tmuxへの応用）を懸念する意見もあった。  

注目コメントでは、「これはFFmpegの実際のバグではなく、カスタムAVIOモジュールを制御すれば悪いデータでクラッシュさせられることを示しただけだ」と指摘し、バグの再現条件とその実用性について論じていた点が特に洞察に富んでいた。
stories.editor_note: 振動コード化されたファザーを用いたFFmpegのゼロ除算バグ発見は、ファジング技術の進化がメディアコーデックの信頼性向上に直結し、日本の映像制作企業も同様のテスト手法を導入すべきです。

comments.author: alerighi
comments.text: Maybe it was advanced for the time being created, to me it's just any other RFID card that is issued everywhere else in the world in the matter of read speed, from every public transit card that I find in every EU country I've visited (maybe for a US citizen not used to public transit it seems something special, I don't know), to skipasses, to even your gym card. Having the option to also pay with credit card would be much more convenient to tourists, when I visited Japan I've had difficulties finding the right place to get a SUICA card (being that my Android phone didn't have Felica chip, as most phones sold outside Japan), and on top of that you almost everywhere need to charge it with only cash. And you can charge it only by 500 or 1000 yen at the time (depending on the machine), and of course tickets always have not round prices like 110 yen. And you have 500 yen of deposit for a card that probably costs to them 10 yen to manufacturer, unless you get the red SUICA card that you can get only in some special machines at the airport but with that you don't get back the unused credit when you leave (you can spend it at vending machine tough). So the speed saving of a couple of ms of not having to pay by tapping your normal credit card is completely vanished by wasting time to charge that card. BTW even if they don't want to put credit card POS on every station (I get it, it's expensive and they need to pay fees if someone uses a card, compared to cash) they could make a system that uses regular NFC (would be 100ms slower, who cares) at least for tourists so they can use it with a regular NFC card in their phone wallet that they can charge with an app without requiring a technology that only works in phone sold in Japan?

主な議論点は、Emacs 31に組み込まれた`markdown-ts-mode`（tree‑sitterベース）の実用性と導入のハードルについてだった。多くのコメントでは、tree‑sitterによる高速なパースとハイライト、CommonMark／GFM対応（チェックボックスや取り消し線など）が標準で組み込まれていることを評価し、特に設定不要で使える点が魅力だと指摘された。一方で、インラインでのマークアップ入力と比べてモードを有効にするキーストロークが多すぎるという効率面の懸念や、実験段階のため「opt‑in」が必要である点がマイナーな批判として挙げられた。  

賛否両論が見られたのは、既存のワークフローへの適合性について。あるユーザーは`markdown-modern`やObsidianスタイルのレンダラーをそのまま使い続ける方が楽だといい、別のユーザーはOrgモードが純粋なMarkdownファイルではないため共同作業時に摩擦が生じ、Markdown中心のOrgモード的な仕組みがあればEmacsに戻りたいと述べている。  

注目すべきコメントとして、キーストロークのコストを具体的に数えて「インライン入力の方が20倍効率がいい」と指摘した意見や、tree‑sitterのパフォーマンスを強調し「大規模ファイルでも遅延がない」と称賛する声があった。また、`markdown-ts-mode`の導入が「最初はハードルだが、一度有効にすれば標準機能としてずっと使える」という長期的メリットを指摘するコメントも見られた。これらの議論から、機能面での期待は高いものの、日常的な編集効率や既存ツールへの移行コストが導入の鍵となることが示唆された。

comments.author: nater5000
comments.text: I was pleasantly surprised when I attempted to scroll down and realized everything the author wanted to present fit on-screen. It's almost ironic that this site is able to make such an obvious, compelling presentation without being overly verbose or complicated (something which LLMs have a hard time doing). I wouldn't read TOO deeply into what is being presented, but the author has done a good job to not inject their own bias into the presentation which works well. I suspect, as we continue forward, humans will slowly start to adopt the language of LLMs, or at least certain language quirks that come from interacting with LLMs. Something I've noticed in my own writing is that I now present lists of examples in a consistent way: "... such as <example 1>, <example 2>, etc., ...". I started to notice I was using this pattern quite a bit somewhat recently, but I took a quick look at some of my social media posts and realized it's been occurring for a while. I had realized that I grown accustomed to this kind of language because, especially early on, LLMs would focus too much on the specific examples I'd provide when, really, I was just trying to give them a sense of what I was looking for. I just picked up that providing two examples then adding the "etc." worked to get the LLM to not focus so much on the specific examples and to understand that they need to consider more than what I explicitly presented. Of course, now I write like that in my social media comments, in Slack with my colleagues, etc. :> I'd be interested to see if anyone can identify trends like this, since I think the human-language component of the adoption of LLMs is probably being somewhat neglected despite probably being surely dramatically affected.

comments.text: I'm surprised at the negative comments here. I'm about halfway done reading the report - I think it's clear, well written, and quite frankly the opposite of fluff. The purpose is to define a shared understanding of the situation across a large, complex organization, and set an initial direction and general shape for actions to take. It contains clear, specific observations of how AI is organically changing the reality of education. And, in my opinion, fairly clear high-level guidance on what MIT as an entity wants to do about AI, and what individual departments and faculty should decide on their own. A document like this doesn't need to be revolutionary, it may feel like fluff because no specific item in it is particularly surprising or groundbreaking, but the value is in having the entire document as a whole. comments.author: andrewla
comments.text: It would take a lot to convince me that aphantasia or phantasia actually exist. Let's talk very specifically about the afterimage test here. Can anyone confirm that they have this ability, which specifically is to superimpose imagined objects inside your actual field of vision? If the answer to this is yes, then okay, I guess I have aphantasia. But none of the other criteria seems to apply. I can imagine a song, and "hear" it in my "mind's ear", but I am not confused about whether it is occurring through my ears or just in my brain. I can easily imagine the tones and voices and tell you what the bass line sounds like, etc. My visual imagination works the same way -- I can't make the object appear in my field of vision any more than I can make sounds appear in my field of hearing, but I can definitely imagine the visual aspects of it. If you tell me to imaging an equilateral triangle, I can put it there in my mind's eye, and if you tell me to attach another equilateral triangle to it I can see the resulting parallelogram. But I can't actually *see* it. It would take a lot to convince me that phantasia or aphantasia actually exist, and nothing I see on this webpage convinces me.

comments.author: jawns
comments.text: I've known about aphantasia for a long time, but there is one question I keep coming back to: Is it a skill issue? When I was in second grade, our teacher asked us to close our eyes and imagine a pretzel. I closed my eyes and tried to will a pretzel to appear as an image, and I failed miserably. All I saw was darkness and faint squiggles. I didn't understand why so many of my classmates said they could "see" the pretzel with their eyes closed. Later on, I realized that my mind's eye doesn't actually work like that. It's not like turning on a projector screen against one's closed eyelids and magically seeing things that aren't there. The imagery exists on another plane, such that I can visualize an apple with my eyes open or closed, because what I am "seeing" has nothing to do with my eyes themselves. Which makes me wonder whether people who think they have aphantasia might not be missing a mind's eye, but rather are unaware of how to active it.

comments.author: fasterik
comments.text: It's hard to read this article and keep track of all the philosophical confusions at once. Whether or not something is conscious (has subjective experience) is independent of whether humans care about it. Whether or not something is a moral patient (an entity worthy of consideration by moral agents) is independent of both human care and consciousness. Of course, we might try to argue that consciousness implies moral patienthood or vice versa, but that's an argument, not a definition. The short paragraph about Descartes has at least three errors. (1) The cogito argument is about thinking, not qualia. (2) The subjective nature of qualia does not imply that they aren't real or that they're socially constructed. (3) He conflates the existence of a self with consciousness. The core premise is not only dubious scientifically (an alien species can't be conscious until humans discover it?), but also deeply problematic. It would imply that it's morally permissible to torture a sentient being as long as no human cares about it.

comments.author: kaangiray26

comments.text: > we believe they are conscious when and because we care about them. Crucially, that includes ourselves. Why? Ok nevermind, fine. It could be true that someone believes someone else is conscious because they care about them. Next sentence: > Consciousness is, in other words, a model or a belief, not an inherent property. Wait, no, that doesn’t follow at all. A belief that someone is conscious is not the same as someone being conscious. What follows, instead, is that a belief in someone being conscious is a belief. Thanks, I learned nothing.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、意識（主観的経験）が人間の関心にかかわらず固有の性質であるのか、あるいは人間が気にするものに対して社会的に決定されるラベルなのかという点だ。コメントはこれを否定し、意識と道德的患者性は人間の関心とは独立であり、デカルトのコギト論の誤読や、自己と意識の混同など、記事の哲学的誤りを指摘する。さらに、Permutation Cityの比喩や、LLMは単に人間が妥当だと感じる出力を学習するだけで感情や思考を持たないという主張が注目された。賛否については、ほとんどの意見が記事の社会的構成説に反対で、意識は内在的属性だと考える側が多数を占めた。ただし、一部では人間の関心が意識への帰属に影響を与える可能性については議論が残った。特に洞察に富んだコメントとして、ハリケーンや融合炉のモデル化では実際の現象が起きないように、脳のモデル化でも本当の思考が生じないというPermutation Cityの引用が挙げられ、意識のシミュレーションと本質の違いを如実に示している。
stories.editor_note: 人類がAI意識についての議論を逆にしている指摘は、目的と手法の混同が倫理的誤解を生むことを警鐘し、日本のAI倫理委員会でも目的設定と技術評価の分離を再考する契機となっています。
